title: Logistic Regression Hyperparameters
abstract:
The three hyperparameters that matter — C, penalty and
max_iter — plus the solver constraints that quietly determine which
combinations are even legal. The critical point is that C is the
inverse of the regularisation strength, so smaller means stronger, which
is the opposite of every $\lambda$ you have met so far. This document covers each
parameter, the solver compatibility table, class_weight for imbalanced
data, and how to tune them together.

blocks.t: The Three That Matter
From the notes: important only

items:
Regularization strength — controls how much
 regularization is applied. $C=\dfrac{1}{\lambda}$, so a smaller $C$
 means stronger regularization means a simpler model, and vice versa.
 Default $=1.0$.

Type of regularization: $\ell_1$, $\ell_2$,
 elasticnet, none. Default $=\ell_2$.

blocks.t: C — and the Inverse Convention
The single most common confusion in scikit-learn

Everywhere in Topics 41–43 the regularisation strength was $\lambda$, and
larger $\lambda$ meant more regularisation. Logistic regression and
SVMs use $C=1/\lambda$ instead, so the direction is reversed:
Setting C=100 thinking you are regularising heavily does the opposite.
Where $C$ sits in the objective

\min_{w,b} \underbrace{\tfrac{1}{2}w^{ \top}w}_{\text{penalty}}
 + C\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log \left(1+e^{-y_i(w^{ \top}x_i+b)}\right)

Note that $C$ multiplies the loss, not the penalty. So a large $C$ makes
the data term dominate — fit the training points closely — while a small $C$
makes the penalty dominate — keep the weights small. Dividing through by $C$
gives the familiar $\text{loss}+\lambda\|w\|^2$ form with $\lambda=1/C$.

blocks.t: Regularisation is on by default

scikit-learn applies $\ell_2$ with $C=1.0$ unless you say otherwise. This is
deliberate: it prevents the weights from diverging under perfect separation
(Topic 46), and it means LogisticRegression() is not plain maximum
likelihood. To get the unregularised fit, pass penalty=None.

Penalty
Effect

Drives some weights to exactly zero — feature selection (Topic 42)
Pure maximum likelihood. Diverges under separation

Not every combination is legal, and the error message is not always obvious:

If you want $\ell_1$ or elastic net, you must switch to saga (or
liblinear for $\ell_1$).
max_iter

blocks.cap:
Left: accuracy against the iteration budget — below the convergence
 point the model has simply stopped early. Right: solver timings on the same
 problem.

blocks.t: What a ConvergenceWarning actually means

There is no closed form for logistic regression (Topic 46), so it is fitted
iteratively. max_iter=100 is a budget, not a target. If the
optimiser exhausts it, scikit-learn warns — and the model you get is whatever
the optimiser had reached, which may be far from optimal.
Three responses, in order of preference:

items:
Scale the features. Poor conditioning is the usual cause
 (Topic 37); scaling often fixes it in one line.

Increase regularisation (lower $C$), which makes the problem
 better conditioned.

blocks.t: Suppressing the warning is not one of them.
Two More Worth Knowing

rows: "balanced" weights each class by $n/(C\cdot n_c)$, so the minority class contributes as much total weight as the majority. Essential for imbalanced data (Topic 80) — and it changes what the model optimises, unlike moving the threshold
"multinomial" uses softmax (Topic 50); "ovr" fits one binary model per class. Multinomial is the principled choice for mutually exclusive classes

blocks.t: Scaling is a hyperparameter decision too

Because the $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ penalties treat all coefficients alike but a
coefficient's magnitude depends on its feature's units, regularised
logistic regression requires standardised features for exactly the reasons given
in Topic 41. Without scaling, how much each feature is penalised is an artefact of
your unit choices — and the solvers converge far more slowly.
Code

import numpy as np, warnings
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.model_selection import (cross_val_score, GridSearchCV,
                                     train_test_split)
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report, recall_score

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, p = 800, 25
X = rng.normal(0, 1, (n, p))
w = np.zeros(p); w[:4] = [2.5, -2.0, 1.5, 1.8]          # only 4 real features
y = (X @ w + rng.normal(0, 1., n) > 0).astype(int)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=.3, random_state=0)

# =====================================================================
# 1. C IS THE INVERSE OF LAMBDA -- smaller C = STRONGER regularisation
# =====================================================================
print(f"{'C':>10s} {'lambda=1/C':>12s} {'sum |w|':>10s} {'train':>8s} {'cv':>8s}")
for C in [1e-4, 1e-2, 1e-1, 1.0, 1e2, 1e4]:
    m = LogisticRegression(C=C, max_iter=8000).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    cv = cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(C=C, max_iter=8000),
                         X_tr, y_tr, cv=5).mean()
    print(f"{C:10.0e} {1/C:12.0e} {np.abs(m.coef_).sum():10.3f} "
          f"{m.score(X_tr, y_tr):8.4f} {cv:8.4f}")
# Small C -> tiny weights -> underfitting.
# Large C -> big weights  -> overfitting.
# THE OPPOSITE DIRECTION TO Ridge's alpha.

print("\nC=0.0001 predicts almost everything as the base rate:",
      LogisticRegression(C=1e-4, max_iter=8000).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
      .predict_proba(X_te)[:3, 1].round(4))

# =====================================================================
# 2. REGULARISATION IS ON BY DEFAULT
# =====================================================================
default = LogisticRegression(max_iter=5000).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
none_   = LogisticRegression(penalty=None, max_iter=5000).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print(f"\ndefault (l2, C=1) sum|w| {np.abs(default.coef_).sum():.3f}")
print(f"penalty=None      sum|w| {np.abs(none_.coef_).sum():.3f}")
print("-> LogisticRegression() is NOT plain maximum likelihood")

# And that default is what keeps the weights finite under separation:
Xs = np.array([[1.], [2.], [3.], [8.], [9.], [10.]])
ys = np.array([0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1])                        # perfectly separable
with warnings.catch_warnings():
    warnings.simplefilter("ignore")
    print(f"\nseparable data, C=1     : coef {LogisticRegression(C=1).fit(Xs,ys).coef_[0][0]:8.3f}")
    print(f"separable data, C=1e6   : coef {LogisticRegression(C=1e6, max_iter=50000).fit(Xs,ys).coef_[0][0]:8.3f}")
    print(f"separable data, no penalty: coef "
          f"{LogisticRegression(penalty=None, max_iter=50000).fit(Xs,ys).coef_[0][0]:8.3f}")
# Without regularisation the coefficient runs away (Topic 46).

# =====================================================================
# 3. penalty -- and the SOLVER CONSTRAINT
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'penalty':>12s} {'solver':>10s} {'cv acc':>9s} {'non-zero':>10s}")
configs = [("l2",         "lbfgs",     {}),
           ("l1",         "saga",      {}),
           ("elasticnet", "saga",      {"l1_ratio": 0.5}),
           (None,         "lbfgs",     {})]
for pen, solver, extra in configs:
    with warnings.catch_warnings():
        warnings.simplefilter("ignore")
        kw = dict(penalty=pen, solver=solver, max_iter=8000, **extra)
        if pen is not None:
            kw["C"] = 0.1
        m = LogisticRegression(**kw)
        cv = cross_val_score(m, X_tr, y_tr, cv=5).mean()
        m.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    print(f"{str(pen):>12s} {solver:>10s} {cv:9.4f} "
          f"{int((np.abs(m.coef_) > 1e-8).sum()):10d}")
# l1 zeroes most of the 21 noise features; l2 keeps all 25.

# The illegal combination fails loudly:
try:
    LogisticRegression(penalty="l1", solver="lbfgs").fit(X_tr, y_tr)
except ValueError as e:
    print("\nlbfgs + l1:", str(e)[:75])
try:
    LogisticRegression(penalty="elasticnet", solver="liblinear",
                       l1_ratio=.5).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
except ValueError as e:
    print("liblinear + elasticnet:", str(e)[:75])

# =====================================================================
# 4. max_iter -- a ConvergenceWarning means it STOPPED EARLY
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'max_iter':>9s} {'n_iter_':>9s} {'converged':>11s} {'train acc':>11s}")
for mi in [1, 5, 20, 100, 500, 5000]:
    with warnings.catch_warnings():
        warnings.simplefilter("ignore")
        m = LogisticRegression(max_iter=mi, C=1.0).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    print(f"{mi:9d} {int(m.n_iter_[0]):9d} "
          f"{str(int(m.n_iter_[0]) < mi):>11s} {m.score(X_tr, y_tr):11.4f}")
# n_iter_ == max_iter means the budget was exhausted, NOT that it converged.

# THE USUAL FIX IS SCALING, NOT A BIGGER BUDGET:
X_bad = X_tr.copy(); X_bad[:, 0] *= 10_000              # badly conditioned
with warnings.catch_warnings():
    warnings.simplefilter("ignore")
    a = LogisticRegression(max_iter=100).fit(X_bad, y_tr)
    b = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                      LogisticRegression(max_iter=100)).fit(X_bad, y_tr)
print(f"\nunscaled: n_iter {int(a.n_iter_[0])} (budget 100)")
print(f"scaled  : n_iter {int(b[-1].n_iter_[0])} (budget 100)  <- converges easily")

# =====================================================================
# 5. class_weight FOR IMBALANCED DATA
# =====================================================================
n2 = 4000
X2 = rng.normal(0, 1, (n2, 6))
pr = 1/(1+np.exp(-(2.5*X2[:, 0] + 1.5*X2[:, 1] - 5.0)))
y2 = (rng.random(n2) < pr).astype(int)
X2tr, X2te, y2tr, y2te = train_test_split(X2, y2, test_size=.3,
                                          stratify=y2, random_state=0)
print(f"\npositive rate: {y2.mean():.3%}")
for cw in [None, "balanced"]:
    m = LogisticRegression(class_weight=cw, max_iter=5000).fit(X2tr, y2tr)
    pred = m.predict(X2te)
    print(f"class_weight={str(cw):>9s}  accuracy {m.score(X2te,y2te):.4f}  "
          f"recall {recall_score(y2te, pred):.4f}  "
          f"predicted positive {int(pred.sum()):4d}")
# 'balanced' trades accuracy for recall. Note this changes what the model
# OPTIMISES -- unlike moving the threshold, which changes only the decision.

# =====================================================================
# 6. TUNE THEM TOGETHER
# =====================================================================
grid = [
    {"logisticregression__solver":  ["lbfgs"],
     "logisticregression__penalty": ["l2"],
     "logisticregression__C":       np.logspace(-4, 4, 17)},
    {"logisticregression__solver":  ["saga"],
     "logisticregression__penalty": ["l1"],
     "logisticregression__C":       np.logspace(-4, 4, 17)},
    {"logisticregression__solver":   ["saga"],
     "logisticregression__penalty":  ["elasticnet"],
     "logisticregression__l1_ratio": [0.2, 0.5, 0.8],
     "logisticregression__C":        np.logspace(-3, 3, 9)},
]
with warnings.catch_warnings():
    warnings.simplefilter("ignore")
    gs = GridSearchCV(
        make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                      LogisticRegression(max_iter=8000)),
        grid, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc", n_jobs=-1).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print("\nbest:", {k.split("__")[-1]: v for k, v in gs.best_params_.items()})
print(f"cv auc {gs.best_score_:.4f}   test auc "
      f"{gs.score(X_te, y_te):.4f}")
print(f"default C=1.0 test auc: "
      f"{make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=5000)).fit(X_tr,y_tr).score(X_te,y_te):.4f}")
# Note the grid is a LIST of dicts -- that is how you express the
# solver/penalty compatibility constraints to GridSearchCV.
Worked Examples
What the parameter $C$ actually trades off

In scikit-learn, LogisticRegression minimises $\tfrac12\|w\|^2 + C\sum_i \text{logloss}_i$. Large $C$ means weak regularisation; small $C$ means strong regularisation. Compare two candidate weight vectors on the same data:
At $C=0.1$, B wins (1.5 $<$ 12.7): the penalty dominates, so the simpler model is preferred.
Now at $C=10$:
A wins: the data term dominates, so the better fit is preferred.
Rule. Smaller $C$ = more regularisation = smaller weights = simpler boundary. Tune $C$ on a log scale (for example $10^{-3}$ to $10^{3}$) with cross-validation, not by intuition.
Summary
Everything on one page

items:
C — regularisation strength. $C=1/\lambda$, so a
 smaller $C$ means stronger regularisation and a simpler model,
 and vice versa. Default $1.0$. This is the opposite
 direction to Ridge's alpha.

In the objective, $C$ multiplies the loss, not the penalty —
 which is why large $C$ means "fit the data closely".

penalty — type of regularisation: $\ell_1$, $\ell_2$,
 elasticnet, none. Default $\ell_2$. $\ell_1$ additionally does
 feature selection.

Regularisation is applied by default, which is what keeps the
 weights finite under perfect separation. penalty=None gives plain
 maximum likelihood.

The solver constrains the penalty. lbfgs supports only
 $\ell_2$/none; saga is the only solver supporting elasticnet.

max_iter — maximum iterations for convergence.
 Default $100$. A ConvergenceWarning means the budget ran out, not that
 the model is fine. Fix by scaling first, then raising the budget.

class_weight="balanced" is the standard lever for imbalanced data;
 it changes what the model optimises.
Regularised logistic regression requires scaled features.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. What does C do in LogisticRegression?

It is the inverse regularisation strength, $C=1/\lambda$. Smaller $C$ means
stronger regularisation and a simpler model — the opposite direction to
alpha in Ridge and Lasso. In the objective, $C$ multiplies the loss term,
so a large $C$ tells the optimiser to fit the training data closely.
Q. Is LogisticRegression() unregularised by default?

No. scikit-learn applies $\ell_2$ with $C=1.0$. That default exists because
without it the weights diverge on separable data. Pass penalty=None for
true maximum likelihood.
Q. You want $\ell_1$ but get a ValueError. Why?

The default solver lbfgs does not support $\ell_1$. Switch to saga
(or liblinear). Only saga supports elasticnet.
Q. You get a ConvergenceWarning. What do you do?

Scale the features first — poor conditioning is the usual cause and scaling
usually fixes it outright. Then raise max_iter. Increasing regularisation
also helps by improving the conditioning. Do not simply silence the warning: the
model returned is whatever the optimiser had reached when the budget ran out.
Q. class_weight="balanced" or moving the threshold?

They are different interventions. class_weight changes the loss,
so the model is trained differently and its probabilities are re-calibrated to the
weighted problem. Moving the threshold leaves the model untouched and changes only
the decision rule. If you want calibrated probabilities plus a chosen operating
point, train unweighted and move the threshold.
Q. How do you tune these together given the solver constraints?

Pass GridSearchCV a list of parameter dictionaries, one per valid
solver/penalty combination. That expresses the compatibility rules directly
instead of generating illegal combinations.
